articles.body: A cough in a young child is often linked to a cold, allergies or asthma. But when it persists, returns repeatedly or comes with unusual tiredness and breathlessness, it deserves closer attention. The tragic death of three-year-old Penny Dunn in England has renewed questions about recognising less obvious signs of serious illness in children.Penny’s mother, Courtney Sherwood, is now urging parents to trust their instincts when something about their child’s health does not seem right.Penny Dunn’s cough did not go awayAccording to Kennedy News and Media, Penny developed a cough around Christmas 2025. The three-year-old, who lived in Gloucestershire, England, had reportedly been healthy and rarely ill before then.Her mother, 27-year-old Courtney Sherwood, said the cough briefly improved before returning and becoming persistent. She and Penny’s father took her to the doctor three times. The family was initially told that Penny had a childhood bug, while asthma was also considered.The cough eventually became severe enough to make Penny vomit. Sherwood also noticed that her daughter became unusually breathless, including after climbing the stairs to the doctor’s office. Inhalers appeared to help for a time, according to the mother.But Penny’s health continued to decline. Sherwood said her once-active daughter became lethargic, refused food and appeared to be losing weight.Seizure led to the discovery of a serious heart problemOn June 29, Penny suffered a seizure while taking part in a sports day at nursery school. Doctors found that her heart was enlarged and beating abnormally. It was also struggling to pump blood effectively.Penny was transferred to another hospital after medication failed to stabilise her condition. She was placed on advanced life support and diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM).DCM causes the heart’s chambers to enlarge, while the heart muscle becomes stretched and weaker. This can reduce the heart’s ability to pump blood and may lead to heart failure or abnormal heart rhythms.Penny also underwent surgery to address the abnormal rhythm. Her family initially hoped she would recover, but further complications followed. CT scans showed that parts of her brain and bowel had died after losing adequate blood supply.Doctors told her parents that she would not have a meaningful quality of life if she survived. The family eventually decided to withdraw life support. Penny died on July 6.Sherwood said she did not blame the medical team and described the doctors as phenomenal. She also said the cause of Penny’s illness remained unclear, although doctors told the family that a cold might have triggered it.When should a cough raise concern about the heart?Dr Manish Bansal, Vice Chairman, Cardiac Care, Clinical & Preventive Cardiology, Medanta Gurugram, said parents should not automatically assume that a persistent cough is a respiratory problem.“I would caution parents against assuming that a persistent cough is always a respiratory problem. In most cases, cough in children is caused by infections, allergies or asthma, but when it is prolonged, recurrent or accompanied by breathlessness, unusual fatigue, poor exercise tolerance, swelling, excessive sweating or difficulty feeding, it deserves a closer medical evaluation.”He explained that some heart conditions can increase pressure in the lungs or cause fluid congestion when the heart cannot pump blood efficiently. This can sometimes produce symptoms that resemble a respiratory illness.However, a cough alone does not mean a child has heart disease. The important concern is a persistent or unexplained pattern, especially when the child’s energy, growth or usual activity changes.What parents should know about testingDr Bansal said a clinical examination can help doctors decide whether further heart investigations are needed, “A thorough clinical examination, followed when indicated by investigations such as an echocardiogram or ECG, can help identify whether there is an underlying cardiac issue.”An ECG records the heart’s electrical activity, while an echocardiogram uses sound waves to examine the heart’s structure and pumping function.Dr Bansal stressed that awareness should not become panic, “The key is awareness rather than alarm. Parents know their child’s normal behaviour best, and any significant or unexplained change should prompt timely consultation with a doctor.”For Sherwood, that message carries a deeply personal meaning. After losing Penny, she has called for greater access to heart testing in children’s primary care settings and encouraged parents to seek a second opinion when something feels wrong.Medical experts consultedThis article includes expert inputs shared with TOI Health by:Dr Manish Bansal, Vice Chairman, Cardiac Care, Clinical & Preventive Cardiology, Medanta Gurugram.Inputs were used to explain when a persistent cough in children may signal an underlying heart condition and why parents should seek timely medical evaluation when symptoms persist or worsen.

articles.title: AI robot for seniors can alert family after a call for help
articles.summary: Tuya Smart's Doova AI home robot rolls to seniors who call for help and connects family via live video, but key privacy questions remain unanswered.
articles.body: If you have a parent or grandparent who wants to stay in their own home, you probably know the question that can sit quietly in the back of your mind: What happens if they fall and nobody realizes they need help? Tuya Smart thinks its small artificial intelligence robot could become part of the answer. The company unveiled Doova at IFA 2026 in Berlin. This wheeled AI home companion is designed for seniors who live independently. It can move through the home, respond when someone calls for help and connect family members through live video when an emergency appears to be unfolding. That gets my attention because Doova goes beyond sitting on a table waiting for someone to press a button or call out from across the room. It can actually come to you. And that raises a bigger question: How much could a robot like this really help someone live safely and independently at home? NEW! Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Health Care With AI In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you take a more active role in your health care. You’ll learn how to organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare questions for your next doctor’s visit. No technical experience is needed. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com THE BEST TIME TO TALK TO YOUR PARENTS ABOUT SENIOR CARE — BEFORE IT'S TOO LATE How Doova responds when a senior calls for help Doova uses LDS LiDAR to navigate around the home. A four-microphone system helps it figure out where a voice is coming from. Meanwhile, AI vision analyzes a person's skeletal posture. If someone falls or needs assistance, they can say, "Hey Tuya, help." Doova then locates the person and rolls over to assess what is happening. Tuya says that if the user does not respond within 60 seconds, Doova starts an emergency response workflow. Family members receive an alert with a two-way live video call so they can see what is happening and arrange assistance. For now, Tuya has not said that Doova automatically detects falls without the user first calling for help or that it directly contacts 911 or a professional monitoring service. So, I would treat it as an added layer of support rather than a replacement for a dedicated medical alert system. Doova wants to be an AI companion too Emergency help is only part of what Tuya has built into Doova. The robot uses a multimodal large language model so people can talk with it in a more natural way instead of memorizing rigid voice commands. For someone spending long stretches at home alone, Doova can carry on a conversation or play entertainment. It can also help make sense of a confusing bill or letter. Another feature caught my eye. Tuya says Doova can identify potential scam risks. YOUR SENIOR PARENTS ARE EASIER TO IMPERSONATE THAN YOU ARE That could be useful for older adults who receive a suspicious message and want a second opinion before responding. However, I would never want someone relying solely on an AI robot to decide whether a bill, email or financial request is legitimate. AI can make mistakes. If Doova flags something suspicious, the safest next move would still be to verify it independently or share it with someone you trust. We've seen how much personal information scammers can gather about older adults, particularly after major life changes such as moving into a retirement community. A WHEELED ROBOT MAY BEAT HUMANOIDS INTO YOUR HOME It can help with everyday routines around the home Doova can remind you to take medication, keep track of your schedule and give you weather updates. Tuya says it can also learn your preferences over time, which could make its suggestions feel more useful day-to-day. The company plans to add a feature that helps find misplaced items around the house. If that works well, I can see the appeal. Plenty of us have spent far too long looking for glasses, keys or a remote that was nearby the whole time. WOULD YOU PAY $8,000 FOR A ROBOT TO FOLD LAUNDRY? Doova can patrol your home while you are away Doova also doubles as a mobile home-monitoring device. Rather than continuously hugging the walls as some patrol robots do, Tuya says Doova travels to selected locations near the center of rooms. From there, it can perform a 360-degree scan. The robot then creates a safety report that can be sent to the user's phone. When the battery runs low, Doova can return to its charging dock on its own. AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU That gives the robot another possible use when someone travels or spends part of the day away from home. However, this capability also leads straight into the biggest question I have about Doova. What about privacy with Doova? Doova has microphones, AI vision and live video inside the home. It can also learn a user's preferences over time. That can make the robot more helpful, but it also means giving it access to a lot of personal information. We raised similar questions when we looked at another AI home robot that can recognize family members and build personalized memories. With Doova, I would want to know where video and audio are processed, what gets stored, who can see it and whether users can permanently delete what the robot has learned. Tuya's launch announcement does not spell out those Doova-specific privacy controls. Until it does, that is something I would look closely at before bringing a camera-equipped AI robot into a loved one's home. You can also review our guide to limiting the information popular AI services collect about you. Doova can control your smart home Tuya also designed Doova to work as a central smart home controller. A senior could use voice commands to adjust connected lights or curtains. Doova can also interact with compatible kitchen and bathroom devices. I like the thinking here. Smart homes can become complicated very quickly, especially when every device has its own app. If Doova can put those controls into a simple conversation, that could make smart home technology far easier to use. The robot has a 10.1-inch HD display with animated facial expressions. Its rounded design also looks more like a friendly household companion than an industrial machine. What we still do not know about Doova There are still some important blanks to fill in. Tuya has not announced a retail price or when consumers will actually be able to buy Doova. I also want to see how it handles a real home. Rugs, cords and tight spaces can trip up mobile robots. Stairs are another obvious challenge for something that moves around on wheels. The bigger question is how dependable Doova would be during an actual emergency. Someone may be frightened, speaking softly or lying somewhere the robot cannot easily reach. That is where real-world testing will tell us much more than a demonstration on the show floor. We reached out to Tuya Smart with questions about Doova's emergency response, privacy protections, connectivity and availability, but did not hear back before our deadline. What this means to you If you are helping a parent or loved one age in place, Doova gives us a pretty good look at where home technology is heading. Instead of relying only on stationary smart speakers or cameras, future AI assistants may move around the house and respond to what is happening nearby. That could give families another way to stay connected while allowing older adults to maintain more independence. However, I would look closely at the emergency process before relying on any product like this. Find out who gets contacted and what happens when the internet fails. You should also understand exactly what the cameras and microphones collect. Finally, think about the person who will actually use it. The best technology in the world offers little value if someone finds it confusing, intrusive or uncomfortable. Kurt's key takeaways What interests me most about Doova is the move from passive smart devices toward AI that can physically come to you. For an older adult who wants to remain independent, having a robot respond to a call for help and bring family into the situation quickly could offer real peace of mind. Still, I would want much more information before trusting Doova with someone I love. Safety technology has to prove itself outside the controlled environment of a trade show. I want to know how reliably it reaches someone during an emergency and how much personal information it collects along the way. The privacy side deserves just as much attention. A moving camera and microphone that learns your routines can become incredibly helpful. It can also become one of the most intimate connected devices in your home. Doova has an interesting idea at its core. Now Tuya needs to show that the technology can earn the level of trust its role requires. Would you put an AI robot with cameras and microphones in an aging parent's home if it could help family respond faster during an emergency, or would that feel like too much surveillance? articles.title: ‘Food divorce’ trend among couples could drive them apart, experts warn
articles.summary: The "food divorce" trend has some couples eating separately, but experts warn the growing trend erodes relationship quality and emotional well-being over time.
articles.body: Between differing diet plans, food intolerances and conflicting work schedules, some couples are choosing "food divorce" — a term circulating on social media for partners who intentionally cook, order and eat their meals separately. While taking separate paths at mealtime might solve logistical headaches, experts warn that splitting up at the dinner table can come at a cost to the relationship. Shared family meals can help people reconnect, build stronger emotional bonds and reduce stress, according to health institutions like Mayo Clinic. ‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT For couples, experts say regularly eating apart could become a concern if it reflects broader emotional distance or reduces opportunities to spend meaningful time together. Nutrition experts emphasize the issue is often less about the food itself and more about the lost opportunity for a built-in daily checkpoint. "I think it reflects many people's very busy schedules," Tanya Freirich, a North Carolina-based registered dietitian nutritionist, told Fox News Digital. "Mealtime can be a time to unite, to communicate, to build social relationships and foster a connection," she said. "If we're eating completely alone or at different times than important people in our lives, it may foster a little bit of disconnection." DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE Eating separately can contribute to a "roommate dynamic," experts note. Without regular time to reconnect and discuss the day, couples may have fewer opportunities for communication. The practice can also contribute to isolation, according to Freirich. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "Communities all around the world for thousands of years have come together around mealtimes," she said. "If so many Americans are eating every meal alone for many days or most of their days, that certainly can't be great for mental health or well-being." There can also be practical drawbacks, as preparing separate meals or ordering from different restaurants may increase grocery costs, preparation time and kitchen cleanup. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Additionally, eating solo can impact individual dietary habits. Studies show people dining alone are more likely to eat quickly, mindlessly scroll on their phones, or settle for heavily processed convenience foods compared to when they share meals with others. "Communities all around the world for thousands of years have come together around mealtimes." Couples can accommodate different dietary needs without preparing entirely separate meals. For those navigating specific calorie targets, plant-based diets or medical restrictions, Freirich recommended building "modular" or "choose your own adventure" meals as a more efficient method. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "Something like a deconstructed taco night, grain bowls, a pasta or noodle night, or even a sheet pan meal where you're creating each food on its own," the expert said. "So the protein, the carb, the veggies are being cooked separately. And then you get to decide your portions and make your own meal from those ingredients that can meet everyone's needs." When conflicting schedules or caregiving duties make daily dinners impossible, experts recommend prioritizing quality over frequency. Even sharing a quick weekend breakfast or setting aside one designated night a week can help maintain connection. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Be very intentional to connect when you can," Freirich suggested. "Make that a really special meal. Be intentional with your connection. Put the phone away and actually enjoy the other person's company."

articles.title: Why are Americans so tired? CDC report highlights who is feeling it most
articles.summary: About 71% of of adults in the U.S. say they experience fatigue, a new report from the CDC found. Women and younger adults are feeling it most often.
articles.body:
The cost of healthcare . Economic uncertainties . Fears of AI-associated end times . It's enough to exhaust anyone.

About 71.5% of adults in the United States say they experienced fatigue on multiple days over the past three months, according to a new report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS). Women and younger adults are more likely to report frequent fatigue, meaning most days or every day, than men are.

Sociologist Natalie A.E. Young, lead author of the report, said fatigue is "one of the most frequently reported health concerns in primary care visits in the U.S." It's the first study about general fatigue from NCHS, which surveyed about 27,000 adults ages 18 and older in 2024 about their health and daily lives.

People with fatigue "are at higher risk of activity limitations and disability, including permanent work disability. Yet there hadn't been much attention to the frequency of general fatigue symptoms in the U.S. adult population," Young said.

Fatigue isn't ordinary sleepiness . It's "physical or mental tiredness or exhaustion that does not improve with additional sleep or rest," the researchers said. General fatigue, which is different from chronic fatigue syndrome , can be a symptom of other health problems or a side effect of medication.

Fatigue is often connected to other health problems, difficulty concentrating and limited social activities. People with symptoms of frequent fatigue were more likely to experience "co-occurring functioning difficulties," including cognitive difficulties, depression and anxiety, said Young.

"So it's not just that fatigue is common," she said. "It's that fatigue is common and those with fatigue are facing limitations in their daily lives."

Adults who experienced frequent fatigue were more than three times as likely to have symptoms of depression and about twice as likely to report cognitive difficulties or symptoms of anxiety, compared to those who don't experience it, the study found.

Nearly 3 in 4 adults felt "very tired or exhausted" at least some days in the past three months.

About 1 in 6 adults experienced frequent fatigue, defined as feeling very tired or exhausted "most days" or "every day."

Frequent fatigue was highest among younger adults, ages 18-34 years (19.5%), with the lowest rate among adults ages 65 and older (12.9%).

Women were more likely than men to report frequent fatigue (20% versus 13%).

American Indian and Alaska Native adults had the highest rate of frequent fatigue (25.5%), followed by white adults (18%), Black adults (17.3%) and Hispanic adults (12.9%), with Asian adults having the lowest rate of frequent fatigue (9.1%).

Adults living in the South (17.7%) and Midwest (17.5%) were more likely to experience frequent fatigue than adults living in the West (15.6%) or Northeast (14.5%), the report showed.

The CDC survey didn't look at underlying causes of frequent fatigue and it doesn't indicate whether it's worse than in previous years.

But Dr. Alana A. Lewis, a cardiologist at the Bluhm Cardiovascular Institute at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago, said the findings were "not unexpected."

"Just living in this country, we all, at some point, feel fatigue," Lewis said.

In the most recent "Stress in America " survey, the American Psychological Association found that a majority of adults reported feeling isolated, left out and more stressed about the future than they used to be.

Stress can cause surges in hormones like cortisol and adrenaline, which can wear a body down. That increasing stress contributes to an uptick in fatigue, said Jennifer Caspari, a clinical psychologist licensed in Denver and Vancouver, British Columbia.

"People are incredibly busy," Caspari said. "They're stressed. They're feeling spread thin. They have a lot on their plates and only so many hours in the day. They're trying to cram in so much."

Stress can also lead to mental health issues like anxiety and depression, which can disrupt sleep, causing us to feel more tired throughout the day, Caspari said.

More than half of women said they felt fatigue "some days," and 20% experienced it "most days or every day."

Caspari said chronic health issues, like autoimmune diseases, which often include fatigue as a symptom, affect women in greater numbers. Hormonal fluctuations during menstruation, pregnancy, perimenopause and menopause can also affect energy levels.

And many women in heterosexual relationships, for example, say they feel they have more responsibilities at work and home than their male partners do, which can lead to them feeling exhausted, Caspari said.

Even when tasks are evenly divided, women experience stress differently. They tend to worry more about organizing and planning and engage in more "internal dialogue" about their responsibilities.

Mental health, lifestyle and physical health are the "three big pillars" that can trigger fatigue, Lewis said. Heart disease, obstructive sleep apnea, anemia and thyroid issues can also be underlying causes of fatigue.

When patients complain of fatigue, Lewis asks:

"Start with the basics," said Lewis, who encourages patients to follow the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 cardiovascular health checklist.

Pay attention to your sleep and stress patterns to determine whether fatigue is a temporary issue or something that's become more "chronic and persistent," which could indicate a medical problem.

Learning to relax, both physically and mentally, is important, said Caspari. Take a break from never-ending to-do lists. "You're not a robot. You only have so much energy," Caspari said.

Passive resting, like sitting down to watch TV, is perfectly fine. Caspari also recommends "active rest," low-intensity activities like breathing exercises and gentle stretching.

"Active rest can feel more nourishing," she said, "and it can have a more helpful impact on the fatigue over time rather than just sitting and scrolling."

articles.title: Omagh: Man charged following armed bus hijacking
articles.summary: The charges include kidnapping, hijacking, aggravated vehicle taking causing injury and possession of an offensive weapon.
articles.body:
A 39-year-old man has been charged with a number of offences after a bus was hijacked in County Tyrone on Saturday .

The driver of the bus was threatened at knife point by a man, who then allowed passengers to leave the bus. However, the bus driver was kept on board.

The charges include kidnapping, hijacking, aggravated vehicle taking causing injury and possession of an offensive weapon.

The man will appear before Enniskillen Magistrates Court on Monday.

Videos circulating on social media appeared to show a Translink Goldliner coach being driven at speed through residential streets while being chased by a Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) patrol car.

Police said the bus was hijacked in the Beltany Road area of Omagh, Co Tyrone, shortly before 13:00 BST on Saturday.

The man who hijacked the bus then made off in the direction of Newtownstewart and a pursuit ensued along the A5 through Victoria Bridge and Sion Mills. The pursuit lasted nearly 20 miles.

"The bus was eventually stopped in the Head of the Town area of Strabane and a man, aged in his 30s was removed from the bus and subsequently arrested," said a PSNI spokesperson.

The Northern Ireland Ambulance Service (NIAS) said two people were taken to South West Acute Hospital for treatment.

articles.title: Popular GLP-1 weight-loss drugs linked to potentially deadly brain disorder
articles.summary: A study linked 15 cases of Wernicke encephalopathy to GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Mounjaro, raising concerns about vitamin B1 deficiency risks.
articles.body: Researchers are warning about a rare but potentially life-threatening brain condition that may be linked to popular GLP-1 weight-loss medications. A new study, published in Clinical Nutrition, identified 15 reported cases of Wernicke encephalopathy, a neurological disorder caused by severe vitamin B1 deficiency, in people taking GLP-1 receptor agonists. Most of the reported cases involved semaglutide, sold under the brand names Ozempic and Wegovy, or tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound. DOCTORS REVEAL HIDDEN DANGER FOR SOME OZEMPIC, WEGOVY USERS WITH BRAIN DISORDERS Researchers found 15 cases through the FDA's Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), published medical literature and their own medical center. Most patients reported gastrointestinal symptoms or nutritional issues, including weight loss, vomiting, loss of appetite or malnutrition, the study noted. Reports of the disorder appeared more often among people taking GLP-1 medications than among those taking other drugs, the researchers found. They emphasized, however, that the study cannot prove the medications caused the condition. Vitamin B1 plays an important role in brain function, the researchers said. Severe deficiencies can cause confusion, trouble walking, balance problems and vision changes. If left untreated, the condition can lead to permanent neurological damage or death. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Karthik Achari, a Chicago-based clinician and founder of PepMD who was not involved in the study, said the findings should be viewed in perspective. "Researchers went through adverse event reports and the medical literature and found a small number of cases, 15, of Wernicke encephalopathy in people taking GLP-1 drugs," Achari told Fox News Digital. "That's out of millions of people on these medications. So this is rare." "But it's real, it's serious, and the mechanism makes sense," he added. GLP-1 medications can reduce appetite while also causing nausea and vomiting, making it easier for some people to become deficient in vitamin B1, Achari said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "The drug shrinks your appetite. It doesn't shrink your body's requirements," he said. "You can now eat very little without feeling it, which is the point of the medication, but your need for protein, vitamins, and fluids didn't go anywhere." People with persistent nausea and vomiting, those losing weight very quickly while eating little, people with a history of bariatric surgery and those who use alcohol heavily may face a higher risk, Achari said. Erin Palinski-Wade, a New Jersey-based nutritionist and author of "The Sleepdemic Solution," said proper nutrition and hydration should be considered part of treatment while taking GLP-1 medications. "GLP-1 medications can dramatically reduce appetite, but that also means people may unintentionally under-eat the very things their bodies need most, especially protein, fiber and fluids," she told Fox News Digital. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Palinski-Wade said ongoing vomiting or diarrhea can increase the risk of dehydration and kidney problems. She urged patients to seek medical guidance if those symptoms continue for roughly 24 hours. "Don't assume every side effect is just part of being on a GLP-1," Palinski-Wade said. "Severe or persistent symptoms deserve attention." The researchers acknowledged that the study relied largely on reports submitted to the FDA and cannot prove GLP-1 medications caused the condition. They called for additional research, and experts said patients should not stop taking prescribed GLP-1 medications based on these findings alone. articles.summary: A 40-year-old woman has died from measles complications in Pennsylvania, marking the state’s third measles-associated death this year as the U.S. experiences its worst resurgence of the highly contagious disease in 35 years.
articles.body: A 40-year-old woman has died from measles complications in Pennsylvania, marking the state’s third measles-associated death this year as the U.S. experiences its worst resurgence of the highly contagious disease in 35 years. The woman, a Jefferson County resident, died on Saturday, county Coroner Greg Furlong said on Facebook. “This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease,” Furlong said. No other information about the woman will be released, he added. The Pennsylvania Department of Health said it was aware of the death reported by the Jefferson County coroner. “The Department of Health is conducting a thorough review of this case and will provide the public with updated information when it becomes available,” health officials said in a statement. At least 676 measles cases have been confirmed in 37 counties in Pennsylvania so far this year, the state’s health officials reported Friday. The outbreak has hospitalized 124 people in the state. Of the confirmed cases, fewer than 1% had been fully vaccinated, Pennsylvania health officials said. The woman is the third person reported to have died in connection with measles in Pennsylvania. The two other measles-related deaths involved infants, according to the Lancaster County coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni. Measles symptoms typically begin with a cough, fever, runny nose and red, watery eyes, followed by a red rash. The disease can cause severe complications, including pneumonia and swelling of the brain. The Jefferson County coroner’s office is working with Pennsylvania health officials on the case, Furlong posted. The U.S. is experiencing its largest measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 3,000 confirmed cases this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

articles.title: DNA test links bike mechanic to Telangana nurse’s rape-murder
articles.summary: DNA analysis by Telangana FSL links mechanic Md Sanaullah to the rape-murder of a 21-year-old Tukkuguda nurse, strengthening police case and charges.
articles.body: HYDERABAD: DNA analysis by Telangana Forensic Science Laboratory (TGFSL) has linked accused Md Sanaullah, 34, to the alleged rape and murder of a 21-year-old nurse at Tukkuguda, providing forensic corroboration to police investigation.Sources in Pahadishareef police said investigators have received the forensic report, which found that the DNA profile generated from biological material collected from the victim’s private parts matched the accused’s DNA profile.Forensic examination of other exhibits collected from the scene also yielded findings supporting the DNA match, sources said. The DNA examination was carried out by TGFSL DNA division.Mechanic lived near victim’s roomSanaullah, a bike mechanic and native of Begusarai district in Bihar, had come to Hyderabad in 2023. At the time of the offence, he was working and staying at a mechanic shop in Tukkuguda, close to the accommodation where the nurse lived.The nurse, who worked at a private hospital in Tukkuguda, was found dead in her room on Aug 29 after colleagues became concerned when she did not respond. Police initially registered a murder case under BNS Section 103 while awaiting forensic findings on suspected sexual assault.Police detained Sanaullah on Aug 30 and later arrested him in the case.Forensics strengthens police caseAccording to investigators, the accused had allegedly been watching the nurse’s movements for nearly a month. Police said he entered her room through a window while she was asleep and attempted to sexually assault her. When she resisted, he allegedly strangled her before escaping through the same window.Following the medical examination, police added rape provisions and sections of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.Investigators had earlier relied on technical evidence, crime scene material, hair strands and other forensic evidence while questioning the accused. articles.title: 'Não largava a mãe', diz tio de menino que morreu atropelado em Maceió | G1
articles.standfirst: Marcos Antônio e a irmã foram atropelados enquanto brincavam em uma calçada no Vergel do Lago. A menina foi atendida e recebeu alta hospitalar. O motorista do carro foi espancado e morreu.
articles.summary: Marcos e a irmã foram atropelados enquanto brincavam no Vergel do Lago. A menina foi atendida e recebeu alta hospitalar. O motorista do carro foi espancado e morreu.
articles.body:
O tio do menino Marcos Antônio Silvestre dos Santos, de 2 anos , morto após ser atropelado enquanto brincava em uma calçada no Vergel do Lago, em Maceió , no domingo (13), disse que a criança era muito apegada à mãe.

“Ele era um menino alegre, com saúde. A mãe não largava ele de jeito nenhum, tinha um cuidado muito grande. A gente não tem nem como descrever esse sentimento entre eles. Ele também era muito apegado à mãe, não saía de perto dela”, lamentou o tio, Manoel Messias Silvestre de Araújo

Marcos Antônio não resistiu aos ferimentos e morreu no local. A irmã dele, Laura dos Santos Macário, de 4 anos, também foi atingida e precisou de atendimento no Hospital Geral do Estado (HGE), mas já recebeu alta.

O motorista do veículo, José Hilton Daltron, de 53 anos, foi espancado e apedrejado por moradores da região . Ele não resistiu e também morreu no local. A Polícia Civil investiga o caso.

Marcos Antônio Silvestre dos Santos, de 2 anos, morreu após ser atropelado em Maceió — Foto: Reprodução/TV Asa Branca Alagoas

Segundo o tio das crianças, Laura está bem fisicamente, mas pergunta pelo irmão. “Ela pergunta o tempo todo onde o irmão está. Eles viviam juntos, brincando”, contou.

O corpo de Marcos Antônio foi levado para o Instituto Médico Legal (IML) de Maceió. A família espera a liberação do corpo, que será sepultado na tarde desta segunda no Cemitério São José, no Trapiche da Barra.

Marcos Antônio morreu e a irmã, Laura dos Santos Macário, ficou ferida após serem atingidos por um carro enquanto brincavam na calçada de casa, no Vergel do Lago, em Maceió.

Testemunhas informaram que o motorista dirigia em alta velocidade e que havia suspeita de que ele tivesse consumido bebida alcoólica. A Polícia Civil investiga as circunstâncias do acidente.

A mãe das crianças, Tainara Michele, contou que a família mora há três anos no imóvel e que era comum os filhos brincarem na calçada de casa. Ela completa 24 anos nesta segunda-feira (14).

“Eu fui estender uma farda da minha filha e ele [o menino] estava na calçada, em um velocípede, brincando com a irmã. De repente aconteceu. A gente levantou o carro, não encontrou ele, mas quando levantamos as pedras, ele estava embaixo”, lamentou Tainara.

Marcos Antônio Silvestre dos Santos — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Moradores reclamaram da falta de sinalização e de equipamentos para reduzir a velocidade dos veículos, como semáforos e sonorizadores, no trecho da Avenida Senador Rui Palmeira onde o acidente aconteceu.

Eles também afirmaram que uma rodovia foi construída em uma rua paralela, mas ainda não foi inaugurada.

O g1 entrou em contato com o Departamento Municipal de Transportes e Trânsito (DMTT) de Maceió, que ficou de apurar a situação.

articles.title: Acidente no Anel Viário de Piracicaba: carro capota na Paterniani | G1
articles.standfirst: Acidente ocorreu na manhã desta segunda-feira (14) no Km 800. Motorista perdeu o controle da direção e capotou. Vítima teve ferimentos leves.
articles.summary: Um acidente no Anel Viário de Piracicaba deixou o trânsito lento na Rodovia Ernesto Paterniani após um carro capotar na manhã desta segunda-feira (14).
articles.body:
Carro capota na Rodovia Ernesto Paterniani e deixa trânsito lento no Anel Viário de Piracicaba — Foto: Edijan Del Santo/EPTV

Um carro capotou na Rodovia Ernesto Paterniani (SPI-162/308) na manhã desta segunda-feira (14). O acidente causou bloqueio parcial do Anel Viário de Piracicaba (SP). Uma faixa da via foi interditada. O trânsito ficou lento no trecho.

A motorista perdeu o controle do carro e capotou. O veículo ficou com as quatro rodas para cima no acostamento da rodovia. A vítima teve ferimentos leves, foi socorrida e encaminhada para o Hospital Unimed.

De acordo com a EPTV , afiliada da Globo para Piracicaba e região, o acidente ocorreu no km 800 da Rodovia, próximo da Hyundai, no sentido Rio Claro (SP).

Um caminhão carregado com 20 toneladas de lixo tombou no km 4 do anel viário de Piracicaba (SP) na tarde de sábado (12). Parte da carga caiu no acostamento da pista.

Segundo informações apuradas no local pela EPTV , o motorista foi encaminhado para a UPA Piracicamirim.

Caminhão com 20 toneladas de lixo tomba no anel viário de Piracicaba — Foto: Edjan del Santo/EPTV

O veículo vinha de Araras (SP) e seguia para Rio das Pedras (SP) quando perdeu o controle e tombou na rotatória.

Equipes da concessionária que administra o trecho foram acionadas para atender a ocorrência. Os agentes bloquearam parcialmente o trecho.

articles.title: Dois homens são presos após bater carro roubado em quatro veículos | G1
articles.standfirst: Prisões foram por roubo de carro, dano e lesão corporal, segundo a PM. Motociclista ficou ferido após ser atingido numa das colisões e foi levado ao Hospital Miguel Arraes, em Paulista.
articles.summary: Prisões foram por roubo de carro, dano e lesão corporal, diz PM. Motociclista ficou ferido após ser atingido numa das colisões e foi levado ao Hospital Miguel Arraes, em Paulista.
articles.body:
Hospital Miguel Arraes, na cidade de Paulista, em Pernambuco. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Dois homens, de 26 e 46 anos, foram presos por suspeita de roubo de carro, dano e lesão corporal no bairro de Maranguape I, em Paulista , no Grande Recife . Um motociclista ficou ferido após os criminosos baterem na moto dele e em outros três veículos na noite do sábado (12).

Após receberem uma denúncia de roubo de carro, agentes do 17º Batalhão da Polícia Militar (PM) encontraram o veículo perto do Shopping North Way, no Centro do município, e iniciaram uma perseguição contra a dupla, que tentou fugir. Após bater nos outros veículos, os dois homens colidiram contra um poste na Avenida Brasil.

De acordo com a PM, os suspeitos estavam com um revólver calibre 32 com cinco munições, duas intactas e três deflagradas. Eles foram encaminhados à Delegacia de Plantão do Paulista.

Em nota, a Polícia Civil afirmou que apreendeu o veículo roubado e um celular. “Os dois suspeitos foram autuados em flagrante e encaminhados à audiência de custódia, ficando à disposição da Justiça”, concluiu a PCPE. Como os nomes dos presos não foram divulgados, não foi possível obter do Tribunal de Justiça de Pernambuco (TJPE) informações sobre o resultado da sessão.

A Prefeitura de Paulista informou, em nota, que enviou agentes de trânsito para remover o veículo roubado e encaminhá-lo à delegacia, além de registrar os sinistros de colisão. Os agentes municipais também organizaram o trânsito no local das batidas.

O motociclista ferido na colisão foi socorrido pelo Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu) e, posteriormente, encaminhado ao Hospital Miguel Arraes, em Paulista. Como o nome do paciente não foi divulgado, não foi possível obter informações sobre o estado de saúde dele.

articles.body: GURGAON: A retired Indian Air Force Group Captain and Kargil War veteran has accused a parking attendant at Magnum Global Park of assaulting him with an iron rod, leaving him with serious head injuries and a fractured hand.In a complaint to police, Group Captain Amit Kumar Gupta (retired) alleged that the attendant also threatened to kill him following an altercation over parking on September 10.The complaint has been lodged in Sector 65 police station.Gupta, who was part of the IAF’s ‘Op Sagar’ team during the 1999 Kargil War, had gone to Magnum Global Park for a family dinner at Gonzo restaurant that night.According to his complaint, Gupta dropped his family at the restaurant around 8pm and went to park his car. articles.title: Woman loses best friend to ovarian cancer, then receives same devastating diagnosis months later
articles.summary: A Minnesota woman diagnosed with stage 3B ovarian cancer after her best friend died from the same disease urges women to advocate for themselves.
articles.body: A Minnesota woman whose best friend died from ovarian cancer was stunned when she was diagnosed with the same disease less than a year later. Becky Drexler was there to support her best friend, Connie Dahl, when she was diagnosed with stage 4 ovarian cancer in April 2015 at age 51. After a courageous battle, Dahl passed away in September 2017. During her friend's cancer fight, Drexler began volunteering with the Minnesota Ovarian Cancer Alliance (MOCA). CANCER SURVIVORS MAY SEE SURPRISING BENEFITS FROM ONE SPECIFIC EXERCISE, STUDY SAYS After retiring in 2017, Drexler was making plans to travel, garden, volunteer and spend more time with family and friends – but those plans were interrupted by her own diagnosis in July 2018. "I was diagnosed with stage 3B high-grade serous ovarian cancer," Drexler, now 65, told Fox News Digital. Like her best friend, Drexler dismissed her own symptoms – including frequent urination, constipation, bloating and hip pain – as common signs of aging. She put off seeing a doctor at first. "By early summer, I felt I was getting signs from Connie to nudge me along," she wrote in an essay sent to Fox News Digital. "Dragonflies represent Connie to me since she passed, and I saw them everywhere. I recall one afternoon being on my patio thinking, ‘Should I go see the doctor?’ when a couple dragonflies in my flower garden just wouldn’t leave me alone. I said out loud, ‘OK, Connie, I’ll go in and talk to the doctor.’" ALCOHOL TIED TO SURPRISING CANCER DEATH PATTERN IN ADULTS UNDER 55, RESEARCHERS FIND On Drexler's 57th birthday, her doctor called to say a CT scan had detected masses on both ovaries. After meeting with an oncologist, she had surgery four days later. Drexler underwent six chemotherapy treatments (carboplatin and taxol) from September 2018 to January 2019. "Those months were difficult but also filled with the support, love and laughter of family, friends, care team and MOCA," she said. "I knew Connie was part of my team as well – just in a different way." Throughout Drexler’s cancer fight, she drew inspiration from her friend’s vow to "be positive, and to live, laugh and love to the fullest every day." "This helped me greatly, as did attending MOCA support group meetings and talking to women who had or were experiencing the same things I was," she said. "There were times I wished Connie was still here so I could talk to her about what I was feeling physically and emotionally." CURE FOR CERTAIN CANCERS IS ‘REALISTIC’ GOAL IN NEXT DECADE, PHARMA LEAD SAYS In August 2020, Drexler’s cancer returned. She had surgery to remove the new tumor from her pelvic area. "We discussed treatment options with my oncologist – she provided the pros and cons of standard chemotherapy, radiation, and no treatment, only monitoring," she shared. "I was diagnosed with stage 3B high-grade serous ovarian cancer." Ultimately, Drexler decided on targeted radiation, with chemotherapy as a backup option if radiation did not work or if there was another recurrence. After radiation was completed in January 2021, Drexler was again considered to have "no evidence of disease" (NED). "I then began taking Lynparza, a PARP inhibitor maintenance treatment – something that was not even available for ovarian cancer patients when Connie was dealing with her cancer," she said. From January 2021 until February 2026, while taking Lynparza, Drexler remained in NED status – "although there was always the concern in the back of my mind about when I would recur again." VISION PROBLEM LEADS TO MAN'S STAGE 4 LUNG CANCER DIAGNOSIS, NEW DRUG EXTENDS SURVIVAL In winter 2026, after experiencing gastric symptoms, Drexler underwent a PET scan. The scan revealed a tumor around her small intestine that had grown large enough to require surgery. "Once the tumor was removed, it was confirmed to be a recurrence of my ovarian cancer," she said. "After recovering from surgery, I had another PET scan, which indicated a couple of spots were still present." In May 2026, Drexler began an 18-week treatment cycle including carboplatin, taxol and avastin, which is expected to be completed at the end of September. "I had a PET scan halfway through (late July), which indicated the treatment is working," she shared. "We were happy to learn that the spots were no longer visible and no new spots had appeared." FDA APPROVES ONCE-DAILY PILL FOR DEADLY CANCER AFTER PATIENTS' SURVIVAL RATES NEARLY DOUBLE Depending on the results of her next PET scan, Drexler said her next treatment will likely be an antibody drug conjugate (ADC) maintenance plan, a recently-approved targeted cancer therapy that has shown "exceptional results." Throughout her cancer journey, Drexler has continued volunteering with MOCA, serving on its board of directors, participating on committees and reviewing grants for ovarian cancer research. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "It does make me think back to when Connie was dealing with her cancer and the treatments that were not available to her but are now available for me and other women," Drexler said. "I believe I am still here because of the advancements in treatments. Developing a reliable early detection test for ovarian cancer remains one of the most critical research goals." Symptoms to watch for Ovarian cancer was once known as the "silent killer," meaning that women would get it and not know anything until the disease was in advanced, more aggressive stages, according to Brian M. Slomovitz, M.D., director of gynecologic oncology at Mount Sinai Medical Center in Miami Beach, Florida. About 75% of women are diagnosed with stage 3 or stage 4 disease, according to the doctor. In recent years, researchers have identified that ovarian cancer actually does have symptoms, noted Slomovitz, who is also deputy director of the Braman Comprehensive Cancer Center. "The problem is they are sort of non-specific symptoms, things that could occur in everyday life – stomach pains, abdominal bloating, things like that." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "There may be an increase in abdominal girth, meaning patients complain that their pants are too tight or they're noticing something different in the way their body's shaped," the doctor said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Those symptoms can also come with weight loss and decreased appetite, he noted: "They could oftentimes mimic gastroenteritis or eating a bad meal." Any symptoms that persist or worsen over a period of one or two weeks should be checked out, the doctor advised. ‘Advocate for yourself’ To other women who may be experiencing worrisome symptoms, Drexler urges them to listen to their bodies. "The early symptoms both Connie and I had were vague, like they are for most women," she said. "They seem like normal things that we can excuse away – we are aging, we are just stressed, we just need to eat better or lose weight." "If something isn’t feeling right or a seemingly minor issue persists, and you think you might be concerned, see your doctor. Advocate for yourself." "They seem like normal things that we can excuse away – we are aging, we are just stressed, we just need to eat better or lose weight." For those who are diagnosed with ovarian cancer, Drexler emphasized that it’s important to see a gynecologic oncologist, as they have additional training in diagnosing and treating cancers. Researchers have spent decades studying early detection and screening for ovarian cancer, Slomovitz said – "but unfortunately, no reliable method has been identified to diagnose women at an earlier stage." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP There is currently no recommended routine screening test for ovarian cancer in women at average risk, because available tests have not been shown to reliably detect the disease early enough to improve outcomes. When ovarian cancer is detected at stage 1, the cure rate approaches 90%, Slomovitz said, underscoring the need for continued research into earlier detection.
